sources.page_text:
Photo of ticks in lab. Photo: Xinhua

A total of 37 people in East China's Jiangsu Province have been diagnosed with Severe Fever with Thrombocytopenia Syndrome (SFTS) this year, a disease caused by the novel bunya virus which is spread by ticks. Experts have warned that the virus can be transmitted from person to person.

Based on previous cases, the virus can be transmitted from infected animals or people to others via blood, respiratory tract and wounds, Sheng Jifang, an expert on the novel bunya virus and director of the infectious disease department with the First Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang University School of Medicine, told the Global Times on Wednesday.

Sheng mentioned that a patient who was infected with the novel bunya virus three years ago and died later had infected 16 people that had contact with the patient's dead body as the patient had bleeding because of severe infection. One of the infected people later died.

Therefore, medical staff and family members of patients should take necessary preventive and protective measures, Sheng said. She also suggested people should not go into the jungle or bushes. "Fortunately, ticks can't fly. It should be safe just to avoid their territory," Sheng said.

Ticks, from larvae to adults, feed on the blood of warm-blooded animals, according to Sheng. Novel bunya virus infections increase significantly in summer when the ticks breed actively. Therefore, the tick-borne virus could possibly cause a local epidemic.

Sheng said the novel bunya virus, which was first discovered in 2009 in Central China's Henan and East China's Anhui provinces has a fatality rate of 1 percent to 5 percent, and older people are more likely to get sick and die. There is no vaccine or specific medicine targeting the infection, so people need to get treatment as soon as possible once they are infected with the virus.

"The early symptoms are fatigue and fever; sometimes there will be a rash," Sheng said.

The clinical manifestations of SFTS mainly include fever, lower quantities of platelets and white blood cells, and multi-organ dysfunction. Patients with mild cases of this disease can mostly heal themselves, but patients with severe cases often suffer from multi-organ dysfunction or even multi-organ failure.

Ticks are mainly found in mountainous regions, as well as areas where there are wild animals, Leng Peien, director of the vector control division with Shanghai's Municipal Center for Disease Control and Prevention, told the Global Times. Some wetlands and forest parks in the city are also habitats for ticks.

So far, the novel bunya virus infections that have been discovered are mainly caused by tick bites, Leng said.

Ticks can carry many disease-causing viruses, such as Lyme disease and Tsutsugamushi disease, Sheng said. The insect is frequently seen in northeastern and southern regions of China.

Lu'an in East China's Anhui Province confirmed on July 11 that the tick-borne infectious disease SFTS has caused five deaths and hospitalized 23 people in Jinzhai county of the city since April. Qingdao in East China's Shandong Province also reported four deaths, according to a media report in July.

sources.page_text:
## Abstract

Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) is an emerging infectious disease that was discovered in China in 2010. The causative agent has been identified as a new member of the Phlebovirus genus in the family Bunyaviridae and has been designated severe fever with thrombocytopenia virus (SFTSV). SFTSV infection can be transmitted person-to-person, and the average case fatality rate is approximately 10% in humans. There is a high seroprevalence of SFTSV infection in a wide range of domesticated animals, including sheep, goats, cattle, pigs, dogs and chickens. Ticks are suspected to be the vector that transmits the virus to humans. Currently, the SFTS endemic area is expanding. Therefore, SFTSV infection is an increasingly important public health threat.

Keywords: bunyavirus, emerging infectious disease, phlebovirus, SFTSV

## Introduction

Since 2009, sporadic cases with clinical presentations of fever (≥38 °C), thrombocytopenia, leukocytopenia and gastrointestinal symptoms were frequently reported in rural areas of Hubei, Henan, Jiangsu, Anhui, Liaoning and Shandong provinces in central and northeastern China. Known pathogens that could cause similar symptoms were not detected in the majority of these patients, and initially the reported case fatality rate was 30%. In response to this emerging infectious disease with unknown causes, enhanced surveillance was implemented for severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) in 2010. More than 20 virus strains were isolated from SFTS patients in six provinces of China, and those isolates were identified as the causative pathogen of SFTS and therefore designated as SFTS virus (SFTSV).1,2 According to the surveillance data,3 SFTS cases have been identified in at least 13 provinces in China, and the average case fatality rate of SFTS is approximately 10%.3,4 Moreover, a newly released report in 2012 revealed that two cases of new phlebovirus infections in Missouri in the United States had clinical presentations similar to those of SFTS, and a phylogenetic analysis showed that the novel virus identified in the United States is most closely related to SFTSV.5

## Morphology and genome structure

Viruses in the bunyaviridae family are generally spherical virions or sometimes are elongated, approximately 80–120 nm in diameter, with a lipid bilayer envelope that is 5–7 nm thick.6 SFTSV virions have typical morphologic features of bunyaviruses. Negative-stain electron microscopy of purified SFTSV virions shows that the virus particles are enveloped spheres or ovals with diameters of 80–100 nm.1 The surface projections could be observed on SFTSV virions, and the typical round and closely packed morphologic units on the virion surface further implicate SFTSV as a member of the phlebovirus genus.7 The interior of the virions, as observed by thin section electron microscopy, has a filamentous or coiled bead appearance, which indicates the presence of a helical nucleocapsid structure comprised of the nucleocapsid protein and the viral genome segments.

Like other members of the family Bunyaviridae, SFTSV is an enveloped RNA virus with three single-stranded RNA genomes, consisting of the large (L), medium (M) and small (S) segments.1 The L and M segments are of negative polarity. The L segment contains 6368 nucleotides with one open reading frame encoding the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRP), composed of 2084 amino acids. The M segment contains 3378 nucleotides with one open reading frame encoding 1073 amino acids of the precursor of glycoproteins Gn and Gc. The S segment of SFTSV contains 1744 nucleotides, which uses an ambisense strategy to encode the nucleoprotein (N) in antisense orientation and the nonstructural protein (NSs) in sense orientation, separated by a 54-bp intergenic region. The 5' and 3' termini of the L, M and S segments possess short noncoding sequences. The 5' noncoding regions of SFTSV strain HB29 are 16 nucleotide (nt) (L), 18 nt (M) and 42 nt (S), and the 3' noncoding regions are 100 nt (L), 141 nt (M) and 28 nt (S).

Phylogenetic trees based on complete sequences of the L, M and S segments, from a panel of SFTSV isolates showed that the novel virus is classified in the genus of Phlebovirus, family Bunyaviridae. Further, phylogenetic analysis of the complete deduced amino acid sequences for the RdRp, glycoprotein (Gn and Gc), N and NSs proteins of six SFTSV strains, showed that all SFTSV isolates were clustered together in comparison with other known Phleboviruses, but were almost equally distant from the other two groups, including the sandfly fever group (Rift Valley fever, Punta Toro, Toscana, Massila, sandfly fever Sicilian viruses) and the Uukuniemi group.1,2 The molecular and morphological data suggested SFTS virus to fit the prototype of a new member of the genus Phlebovirus. A comparison of amino acid sequence similarity provided further support of the separation of SFTSV from other Phleboviruses. Both the RdRp and glycoproteins (Gn and Gc) of SFTSV are slightly more closely related to counterparts in Uukuniemi group but only share a maximum similarity of 36%, while the most highly conserved protein of SFTSV, the N protein, only shared 41% similarity with Rift Valley fever virus (RVFV). With more diversity, the S segment-encoded NSs protein of SFTSV showed the lowest amino acid similarity to RVFV, with a value of only 11%–16%. The pairwise comparisons of SFTSV with the newly discovered Heartland virus in the United States showed that the amino acid sequences of the viral RdRp, glycoprotein (Gn and Gc), nucleoprotein, and non-structural protein shared homology of 73.4%, 62.6%, 62.8% and 63.5%, respectively.1

## Epidemiology and transmission

During recent decades, phlebovirus infections have been mainly recorded in Africa and Europe. For major members of the phlebovirus genus, the phlebotomine sandfly-transmitted viruses (Toscana virus, sandfly fever Sicilian viruses, sandfly fever Naples virus), were reported around Mediterranean Europe; mosquito-transmitted RVFV was reported in Africa and the Arabian Peninsula, and the tick-transmitted Uukuniemi virus was mainly distributed in Europe.6,8,9 There had been no reports of identification of phlebovirus in China until the discovery of SFTSV in 2009.

As a newly identified member in the phlebovirus genus, epidemiological findings revealed that most SFTSV cases occur in farmers living in wooded and hilly areas and working in the fields.1,10,11 There is an obvious seasonal distribution of SFTS: the endemic starts around March, peaks between May and July, and ends around November.1,12 The geographic and seasonal distributions, and the tick bite history of some SFTS cases, suggest that ticks were the insect vector to transmit the virus to humans. Studies showed that the tick species Haemaphysalis longicornis were dominant in the endemic regions, and SFTSV RNA was isolated from approximately 4.9% of the total Haemaphysalis longicornis pools collected.13 The nucleic acid sequences of viruses isolated from ticks has 95% homology with the SFTSV isolated from patients.1 These observations suggest that Haemaphysalis longicornis ticks are most likely the major vector of SFTSV.

Current knowledge suggests that many phleboviruses are maintained in their arthropod vectors by vertical (transovarial) transmission and that the vertebrate hosts play little or no role in the basic maintenance cycle of these agents; however, vertebrate hosts may serve as amplifying hosts. Current studies on domesticated animals reported that 47.7% of the animal sera were positive for SFTSV antibodies,14 and 83% of goats in a county in Shandong Province were seropositive for SFTSV.15 Our seroprevalence investigations of more than 3000 domestic animals, with five species in two epidemic regions, found that approximately 70% of sheep, 60% of cattle, 38% of dogs, 3% of pigs and 47% of chickens were SFTSV antibody positive. However, only a small proportion of studied animals (ranging from 1.7% to 5.3%) were found to carry low levels of viral RNA in sera. A genetic analysis of viral isolates from sheep, cattle, dog, and humans revealed a pairwise distance of the S segment of less than 4.6% (unpublished data). Therefore, it seems that there is an intense epizootic of SFTSV in endemic areas, and the domesticated animals might act as amplifying hosts for SFTSV. However, there is a lack of evidence to confirm vertebrate reservoir hosts and to clarify the possibility of vertical transmission in ticks.

Several studies have provided evidence to highlight the risk of person-to-person transmission of SFTSV through direct blood contact with the patient,10,11,16,17 especially when the index patient has a high virus load in the blood,10 with the virus titer in blood of index patients higher than 107 50% tissue culture infective dose/mL. These reports highlight the need to apply strict infection control for suspected clinical SFTS patients and to emphasize the appropriate use of personal protective equipment (PPE) when treating SFTS patients.

## Clinical features

Most phlebovirus human infections are self-limited, resulting in a mild febrile illness.6 Clinical presentations of SFTS patients are non-specific; major symptoms include high fever, thrombocytopenia, leukocytopenia, gastrointestinal symptoms, and lymphadenopathy. Laboratory tests of SFTS patients commonly show elevated serum alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase (AST), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), creatine kinase (CK), creatine kinase MB fraction (CK-MB) levels, as well as a prolonged activated partial-thromboplastin time. These laboratory parameters are indicative of pathological lesions involved in the liver, kidney and coagulation systems of SFTS patients.1,10,18,19 In severe SFTS patients, the clinical conditions may proceed quickly and end in multi-organ dysfunction syndrome, with clinical presentations of central nervous system (CNS) symptoms and hemorrhagic manifestations. Patients commonly die of disseminated intravascular coagulation and multi-organ failure.1,10,18,19

Dynamic monitoring of the disease course identified three major disease stages of SFTS patients:18 the fever stage, the multi-organ dysfunction stage and the convalescent stage. During the first stage of the disease, day 1 to day 7 post-onset of illness, the initial serum viral load was high (average 105–106 copies/mL) and comparable in both fatal and non-fatal cases. Most SFTS cases in both groups had fever, marked thrombocytopenia and leukocytopenia in this stage. In addition, the alanine aminotransferase, AST, LDH, CK and CK-MB levels began to be elevated later during this stage. The second stage was between day 7 and day 13 post-disease onset. During this stage, the serum viral load decreased in non-fatal cases but still remained high in fatal cases (average 108 copies/mL). Coincident with the respective levels of viral load in non-fatal and fatal cases, the platelet counts reverted to a normal range in non-fatal cases but continued to decline in fatal cases. The levels of the serum enzymes AST, LDH, CK and CK-MB began to decline at approximately day 9 or day 11 in non-fatal cases but progressively increased in fatal cases. When the disease proceeded to the third stage after day 13, for most non-fatal cases, the patients could recover from the disease with most clinical parameters converting to normal. However, for fatal cases, the patients died of severe multi-organ dysfunction syndrome and disseminated intravascular coagulation during this stage, and the serum enzymes reached very high levels before death. The risk analysis revealed that high serum levels of AST (>400 U/L), LDH (>800 U/L), CK (>1000 U/L), and CK-MB (>50 U/L) were risk factors associated with death of SFTS patients.18

In the acute phase of SFTS human disease, the levels of a broad spectrum of serum cytokines, interleukin (IL)-1RA, IL-6, IL-10, granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF), interferon-γ-induced protein 10, and monocyte chemotactic protein-1, were elevated in SFTS patients and were present at higher levels in fatal cases compared to non-fatal cases.19,20 In contrast, levels of the cytokines platelet-derived growth factor-BB and regulated and normal T cell expressed and secreted decreased in SFTS patients. These eight cytokines reverted to normal during the convalescent phase of SFTSV infection. The cytokines IL-1β, IL-8, Macrophage inflammatory protein (MIP)-1α and MIP-1β showed a unique pattern of elevation in fatal cases but not in non-fatal cases. However, the levels of these cytokines increased in the convalescent phase of non-fatal SFTS cases. The regression analysis further revealed that the serum viral load correlated with the serum levels of these cytokines. Moreover, the levels of these cytokines correlated with various clinical parameters.20 These findings suggest that the high viral load may lead to an overproduction of proinflammatory cytokines, which could further exacerbate disease severity. Another study reported the elevation of IL-6, IL-10, G-CSF, interferon-γ, and acute phase proteins (phospholipase A, fibrinogen, hepcidin) in SFTS patients, and a higher production of IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, G-CSF, interferon-γ and phospholipase A in fatal SFTS cases than in non-fatal SFTS cases. The study also showed correlations between the viral load and host biomarkers indicative of fatal outcome, including liver enzymes AST, coagulation factors of activated partial-thromboplastin time, thrombin time and fibrinogen, as well as acute phase proteins phospholipase A and hepcidin.19

## Pathology and pathogenesis in animal models

Currently, an infectious C57BL/6 mouse model with hallmark symptoms of thrombocytopenia and leukocytopenia has been established through intramuscular injection of SFTSV into adult mice. In this murine model, viral RNA was detected in the blood, spleen, liver, and kidney. The humoral immune responses of virus-specific IgM and IgG, neutralizing antibodies, and cellular responses were efficiently induced in the SFTSV-infected mice.21

Histopathological changes were identified in the spleen and bone marrow in the early phase of infection, and pathological lesions in the liver and kidney developed in a later stage. In the SFTSV infected spleen, the lymphocyte cellularity of the red pulp was visually decreased during the first week after inoculation and gradually recovered 14 days later. In addition, a marked increase of megakaryocytes was observed in the spleen. Similarly, megakaryocytes in the bone marrow also significantly increased in the early stage of infection. This increase of platelet progenitor cells in principle and secondary hematopoietic organs suggests extramedullary hematopoiesis may compensate for the depletion of circulating platelets. During the late phase of SFTSV infection, pathological changes were noted in the liver and kidney. The primary lesions in the liver consisted of ballooning degeneration of hepatocytes and scattered necrosis. The lesions in kidney typically included glomerular hypercellularity, mesangial thickening, and congestion in Bowman's space, while infiltration of inflammatory cells was absent. Pathological changes within the liver and kidney tissues were maximal on day 14 post-infection but had nearly recovered on day 28 post-infection. Therefore, the pathological features observed in the spleen and bone marrow during the early stage of infection were consistent with the hematological changes of thrombocytopenia and leukocytopenia.21 The transient pathologic changes observed in kidney and liver at the later stage of infection were indicative of acute glomerular nephritis and acute hepatitis with self-limiting outcomes.

The viral RNA load and infectious titers increased in the spleen on day 3 post-infection, which suggests the spleen as the principle target organ for SFTSV replication.21 Focusing on the spleen, we found that the number of macrophages and platelets dramatically increased in the infected spleen, and SFTSV colocalized with platelets in the cytoplasm of macrophages in the red pulp of the spleen. In vitro cellular assays further revealed that SFTSV adhered to platelets and facilitated the phagocytosis of platelets by macrophages, which, in combination with in vivo findings, suggests that the SFTSV-induced thrombocytopenia was caused by clearance of circulating virus-bound platelets promoted by splenic macrophages. Thus, the study elucidated pathology and pathogenic mechanisms of thrombocytopenia in a murine model that resembles human SFTS disease.21

The SFTSV infection in the established C57BL/6 mouse model could mimic major pathological changes of clinical infection in patients; however, lethal infection has only been induced in certain strains of newborn mice22 but not in adult rodent models. It is suspected that the severe infection could only be induced in immune incompetent hosts, such as newborn mice, without a completely mature immune system, or certain strains of immune-deficient mice.

## Laboratory diagnosis

In most phlebovirus infections, the diagnosis is based on serological tests.8,9 In-house enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) methods are developed, commonly including IgM capture ELISA in acute phase serum or by IgG sandwich ELISA in paired sera from acute and convalescent phases.23 Neutralization assays using early convalescent sera remain the reference method to specifically identify the viruses or to assess the antibody response specificity. Virologic diagnosis of RVFV infection is through detection of viremia in the acute phase of illness, initially using intracranial inoculation into suckling mice or infection of susceptible cells (Vero or mosquito cells) to grow the virus.6 More recently, detection of serum or blood viral RNA copies by reverse transcription-PCR amplification has been developed and was found to be very useful for rapid presumptive diagnosis,24 which could be followed by sequencing to further characterize the viral strains.

Currently, a variety of assays have been developed for laboratory diagnosis of infections with SFTSV. The early viral nucleic acid detection is performed by one-step Taqman real-time assays, using the highly conserved regions of all three genome segments L, M and S of SFTSV as targets.25 Commonly, the viral nucleic acids can be detected in the acute phase serum of patients, within 2 weeks post-onset of the disease. The sensitivity and specificity of the assay is 98.6% and 99%, respectively.25 The real-time PCR assay, based on the S segment, has been approved by the State Food and Drug Administration for application in clinical diagnosis in hospitals and disease surveillance by the local Center for Disease Control and Prevention. With respect to the detection of viral nucleic acids using simple instruments and saving time, a reverse transcription loop-mediated isothermal amplification assay to target eight distinct regions on the S segment of SFTSV has been developed. When combined with a fluorescent detection reagent, visible results could be determined by showing a color change within 30 min.26 Another similar assay, which incorporates reverse transcription-cross-priming amplification with a vertical flow visualization strip based on the M segment of the SFTSV, could complete the entire procedure from specimen processing to result reporting within 2 h.27 As for serodiagnosis, the in-house Mac-ELISA assay, indirect ELISA assay, and double antigen sandwich ELISA assay have been established and optimized to test virus specific IgM, IgG and total antibodies in serum samples of patients, respectively.1,14 Indirect immunofluorescence assays were also established to test the virus specific antibodies using previously fixed SFTSV infected cells on slides. ## Abstract

### Background

Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) incidence has risen steadily in China since the disease was first identified in 2009, with both case numbers and the geographic scope of reporting expanding over time. This study analyzed national surveillance data from 2010 to 2024 to characterize the evolving epidemiological patterns of SFTS.

### Methods

This retrospective descriptive study included clinically diagnosed and laboratory-confirmed SFTS cases from China Information System for Disease Control and Prevention (CISDCP) (2010–2024). Joinpoint regression was used to analyze incidence trends. Case fatality rate (CFR) differences were assessed by chi-squared or Fisher’s exact tests, and the temporal trend was assessed by linear regression.

### Results

During 2010–2024, a total of 30 provinces reported 34,055 cases. From 2010 to 2024, the incidence rate of SFTS in China showed a fluctuating upward trend, with an average annual percent change (AAPC) of 43.28% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 43.23%–43.33%;*P* < 0.01). Most cases were sporadic, with some regional clustering and rapid geographic expansion to previously unaffected areas. The number of reported cases in Anhui Province began to rise rapidly in 2022, making it the province with the highest number of reported cases in China in 2023 and 2024. The average CFR was 4.79%, and the CFR increased with age, reaching 9.15% among those aged 85 years and above.

### Conclusions

During the period from 2010 to 2024, SFTS in China exhibited a marked increase in reported incidence and considerable geographical expansion. The disease is no longer confined to traditional high-risk areas; the rapid rise in cases in province such as Anhui suggests a critical need to re-evaluate the ecological and social factors driving its transmission. Although the overall population CFR showed a declining trend, mortality risk among elderly subgroups still needs attention.

## Background

Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) is an acute viral infectious disease mainly characterized by fever and thrombocytopenia caused by *Dabie bandavirus* (SFTS virus) [1]. It is also characterized by obvious bleeding tendencies accompanied by leukopenia and multiple organ dysfunction [2]. Clinical manifestations are often atypical; no licensed vaccine or specific antiviral therapy is currently available, and clinical management mainly relies on supportive care [3, 4]. SFTS was classified as a nationally reportable disease in China in 2010 and was listed by the World Health Organization(WHO) as one of the top 10 priority infectious diseases in the 2017 annual review of diseases prioritized under the Research and Development Blueprint [5, 6]. The WHO released a prioritization of future pathogens of concern on July 30, 2024, in which the priority pathogens of concern for the Western Pacific region include the *Dabie bandavirus* [7]. This designation underscores the global health importance of SFTS and the need for up-to-date epidemiological data to inform international surveillance efforts. Effective April 1, 2026, SFTS was reclassified as a Class B notifiable infectious disease [8].

Tick bites are the main mode of transmission of the disease. Transmission can also occur through contact with the blood, bloody secretions, excretions, or contaminated materials of infected patients, leading to human-to-human transmission and clusters of cases in household or healthcare settings [9]. People who live and work in mountainous, hilly, or forested areas in endemic regions face a higher risk of infection [10]. Healthcare workers, family members, visitors of patients, and mortuary personnel are at higher risk of infection if they do not adhere to standard protective measures [11].

In addition to China, locally infected cases have been reported in Japan, South Korea, Vietnam, Thailand, Myanmar, Pakistan, and other regions, of which Japan and South Korea have reported the highest number of cases [12,13,14,15,16,17,18]. Due to climate change, there has been an expansion of the potential habitat of ticks to wider geographical locations, posing a risk of introducing the exotic tick species that may carry the SFTS virus [19, 20].

Previous national analyses have characterized the epidemiology of SFTS in China for periods through 2021 or 2023 [21,22,23]. However, no study has examined the complete 15-year surveillance record from SFTS’s initial emergence through 2024, a period that now includes record case and death counts, continued geographic expansion to 30 of 31 mainland provinces. To address this gap, this study analyzed national SFTS surveillance data from 2010 to 2024 to characterize temporal trends, geographic expansion, seasonal patterns, population distribution, time intervals between onset and diagnosis, and case fatality rates (CFR).

## Materials and methods

### Study design

This was a retrospective descriptive study of national surveillance data.

### Data source

SFTS data and annual population data were obtained from the China Information System for Disease Control and Prevention (CISDCP), excluding Hong Kong SAR, Macao SAR, and Taiwan Province [24]. We included cases with onset dates between January 1, 2010, and December 31, 2024. Each case was confirmed by laboratory testing or diagnosed clinically [21, 22, 25]. Case classification followed the diagnosis and treatment scheme for severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (2023 Edition), which had been consistently applied in practice before its official release [26]. The dataset included demographic variables (age, sex, occupation, residence), dates of onset, diagnosis, and death, and case classification.

### Statistical analysis

Data were processed, statistically analyzed, and visualized using Microsoft Excel 2016 and R software (version 4.4.2). No observations were excluded from this analysis.

Joinpoint regression was used to analyze temporal trends in annual SFTS incidence rates. A log-linear model was fitted, allowing a maximum of two joinpoints. The optimal number of joinpoints was selected using the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC). The annual percent change (APC) for each segment was calculated as (exp(β) − 1) × 100%, and the average annual percent change (AAPC) was computed as the weighted average of segment-specific APCs. The 95% confidence intervals (CI) for APCs and AAPC were derived using the Delta method, with statistical inference under the t-distribution. Analyses were performed using R software version 4.4.2.

The onset-to-diagnosis interval was calculated as the number of days between symptom onset date and diagnosis date, as recorded in CISDCP. Given the right-skewed distribution (except in 2010), the median and interquartile range (IQR; 25th percentile [P25]–75th percentile [P75]) were used as summary measures, as they are robust to extreme values.

Deaths were identified based on CISDCP records for reported SFTS cases. The CFR was calculated as deaths/reported cases × 100%. The 95% CI were estimated using the Wilson score method. Group differences were assessed by chi-squared or Fisher’s exact tests, and the temporal trend was assessed by linear regression.

## Results

### National temporal trends

From 2010 to 2024, a total of 34,055 SFTS cases were reported across 30 provinces in China. The number of reported cases (6,602 cases) and deaths (306 cases) in 2024 were both the highest levels since the discovery of this disease, with an increase of 30.4% and 60.2% respectively, compared to the reported cases (5061 cases) and deaths (191 cases) in 2023 (Fig. 1).

Among 34,055 SFTS cases recorded from 2010 to 2024, 21.1% (7,190) were clinically diagnosed and 78.9% (26,865) were laboratory‑confirmed. In 2024, the proportion of laboratory‑confirmed cases reached its highest level at 95.3% (Fig. 2).

**Fig. 2**

Full size image

Classification distribution of SFTS cases in China from 2010 to 2024

From 2010 to 2024, the incidence rate of SFTS in China showed a fluctuating upward trend, with an AAPC of 43.28%, and the difference was statistically significant (95% CI: 43.23%–43.33%; *P* < 0.01). Joinpoint regression identified 2012 as the single inflection point. The incidence rate increased rapidly from 2010 to 2012 (APC = 218.14%, 95% CI: 217.75%–218.52%; *P* < 0.01), followed by a sustained increase from 2012 to 2024 (APC = 14.14%, 95% CI: 14.09%–14.19%; *P* < 0.01).

### Geographic expansion

The geographic range of reported SFTS cases expanded from 17 counties in 5 provinces in 2010 to 459 counties in 24 provinces in 2024, and exhibited geographically discontinuous emergence of reported cases. By 2024, cases had been reported in 30 of China’s 31 mainland provincial-level administrative divisions, with Ningxia being the sole exception, cumulatively affecting 759 counties nationwide (Fig. 3).

**Fig. 3**

### Changes in provincial burden

From 2010 to 2024, cases were mainly concentrated in 7 provinces, including Shandong (9,547 cases), Anhui (7,494 cases), Henan (7,148 cases), Hubei (5,068 cases), Liaoning (1,857 cases), Jiangsu (1,384 cases), and Zhejiang (1,153 cases), with the cumulative number of reported cases accounting for 98.8% of all nationally reported cases. The annual case distribution across these seven provinces exhibited distinct temporal dynamics (Fig. 4). In the early phase (2010–2013), case numbers remained relatively low across all provinces. Shandong and Henan experienced rapid increases beginning in 2014, with Henan reaching its peak during 2015–2016 (976 and 879 cases, respectively). Shandong maintained a relatively high level throughout the period, with a notable surge in 2024 (1,658 cases). The number of reported cases in Anhui Province began to rise rapidly in 2022, making it the province with the highest number of reported cases in China in 2023 and 2024. The number of reported cases in Anhui rose from 544 in 2021 to 841 in 2022, 1,416 in 2023, and reached 1,777 in 2024.

**Fig. 4**

### Seasonal patterns

The incidence of SFTS is seasonal, with a gradual increase in the number of cases from March each year, a peak in May-July, and a decreasing trend thereafter; a secondary increase in case counts was observed in October in some provinces. The cumulative number of reported cases in the months of April-October from 2010 to 2024 was 32,963, accounting for 96.8% of the cumulative number of reported cases in the whole year from 2010 to 2024 (Fig. 5). Different provinces exhibited distinct seasonal patterns. Liaoning showed a later peak (July-September), while Shandong peaked during May-August. A secondary increase in case counts was observed in October in Anhui, Hubei, and Jiangsu provinces.

### Population distribution

Cases were reported in all age groups, mainly in people aged 40–84 years (94.3%), mainly farmers (83.5%), slightly more females than males, and the male-to-female ratio was 0.89:1. The CFR increased with age (Fig. 6). Notably, 37 healthcare workers (0.1%) were among reported cases.

**Fig. 6**

Full size image

Age- and sex-specific distribution of SFTS cases, and age-specific CFR, 2010–2024

### Time intervals between onset and diagnosis

With the exception of 2010 (skewness − 0.12), the distribution of onset-to-diagnosis intervals was right-skewed in all years (skewness range: 2.34–13.97), supporting the use of median rather than mean. The overall median onset-to-diagnosis interval over the 15-year period was 7 days (Interquartile Range [IQR]: 4–11). Annual median intervals and IQRs are shown in Fig. 7. A declining trend was observed from 2010 to 2012, followed by an increase in 2014. From 2015 to 2024, the interval had decreased again, reaching a median of 5 days.

**Fig. 7**

Median onset-to-diagnosis interval of SFTS cases in China, 2010–2024. Shaded area represents the IQR (P25–P75)

### CFR analysis

From 2010 to 2024, a total of 1,632 deaths were recorded among 34,055 reported cases, yielding an overall CFR of 4.79%. The national CFR declined significantly from 12.68% in 2010 to 4.63% in 2024 (linear trend, *P* = 0.004; Fig. 8). The CFR increased with age, from 0.29% in the 30–34 age group to 9.15% in those aged ≥ 85 years (*P* < 0.001). Males had a higher CFR than females (5.41% vs. 4.24%, *P* < 0.001). Laboratory-confirmed cases showed a higher CFR than clinically diagnosed cases (5.55% vs. 1.95%, *P* < 0.001). Substantial provincial variation was observed (*P* < 0.001), with CFRs among seven provinces with the highest case counts ranging from 2.25% (Henan) to 11.97% (Zhejiang).

**Fig. 8**

## Discussion

Compared with previous national analyses covering earlier periods, the present study extends the surveillance period through 2024, capturing the record-high numbers of cases and deaths reported in that year, the emergence of Anhui Province as the leading contributor to the national burden, and the continued geographic expansion.

This study analyzes 15 years of SFTS surveillance data and reveals that SFTS in China is characterized not only by a fluctuating upward trend in reported incidence but also by significant geographical expansion. From 2010 to 2024, a total of 34,055 SFTS cases were reported across 30 provinces. The number of affected counties expanded from 17 in 2010 to 459 in 2024, with a cumulative total of 759 counties ever reporting cases. Both the case count and death count in 2024 reached record highs, with the number of deaths increasing by 60.2% compared to 2023, signaling a worsening disease burden. We note that the observed increase in reported incidence may partly reflect improvements in surveillance sensitivity, diagnostic capacity, and clinician awareness over the 15-year period, particularly during the early years of the study. It is worth noting that this expansion did not spread uniformly but showed characteristics of geographically discontinuous emergence of reported cases. We hypothesize that the geographically discontinuous emergence of reported cases may be driven not only by ecological factors such as climate change, which expands suitable tick habitats, but also by migratory birds and socioeconomic activities such as agricultural trade, which may introduce ticks or infected animal hosts [19, 27, 28]. In 2024, the proportion of laboratory-confirmed cases reached its highest level at 95.3%, reflecting the enhancement of laboratory diagnostic capacity.

Joinpoint regression analysis revealed one inflection point in the incidence of SFTS in China in 2012, dividing the study period into two distinct phases. The rapid increase from 2010 to 2012 (APC = 218.14%) likely reflects, at least in part, the scale-up of surveillance and diagnostic capacity after SFTS was classified as a notifiable disease, rather than a true biological increase in transmission [21]. The period 2012–2024 was a sustained growth phase, with an APC of 14.14%. The increase in cases may reflect the spread of the epidemic, improvements in diagnosis, and the initial effectiveness of comprehensive prevention and control measures implemented in traditional core epidemic areas such as Henan Province [29]. We caution that the AAPC of 43.28% for the entire 2010–2024 period is substantially influenced by the extreme APC during 2010–2012 (218.14%), which reflects improved surveillance sensitivity rather than genuine epidemic growth. The APC for the sustained growth phase from 2012 to 2024 (14.14%) provides a more accurate characterization of the epidemic’s trajectory during the mature surveillance period.

National cases were mainly concentrated in some prefectural cities and counties (districts) in seven provinces, including Shandong, Anhui, Henan, Hubei, Liaoning, Jiangsu, and Zhejiang, which together accounted for over 98.8% of all reported cases. This geographic distribution closely aligns with that reported by Huang et al. for the overlapping period of 2018–2021, supporting the consistency of national surveillance data across analyses [23]. Data from this study show that Shandong had the highest cumulative cases (9,547), followed by Anhui (7,494) and Henan (7,148). The number of cases in Anhui Province increased rapidly starting in 2022, making it the province with the highest number of reported cases in China in 2023 and 2024. This is a significant finding with scientific and early-warning implications. Possible reasons include: climate change leading to environmental conditions in Anhui more favorable for tick vectors and animal host reproduction and virus transmission, or enhanced surveillance and increased awareness among healthcare workers leading to improved case detection [19, 21, 28, 30]. These hypotheses remain to be tested with independent environmental and surveillance quality data. This phenomenon suggests that SFTS risk mapping needs to be dynamically updated, and the allocation of prevention and control resources should not rely solely on historical data but should incorporate meteorological and environmental data to establish an intelligent early warning system.

This study reaffirms the distinct seasonality and population clustering of SFTS. The number of cases gradually increased from March, reached a peak from May to July, and then showed a downward trend. Some provinces had a secondary increase in case counts in October. Consistent with previous research findings [31]. The high-incidence period from April to October represents a critical window for prevention and control. Notably, seasonal patterns varied across provinces. For instance, Liaoning exhibited a later peak (July-September) while Shandong was concentrated in May-August, a secondary increase in case counts was observed in October in Anhui, Hubei, and Jiangsu provinces, suggesting that each province should tailor its prevention and control window accordingly. The population distribution accurately identifies high-risk groups: middle-aged and elderly farmers (40–84 years, 94.3% of cases) engaged in outdoor work with high exposure opportunities [21]. This indicates that future interventions must be highly time-specific and target-specific. For example, concentrated health education and distribution of protective products to farmers in key areas should be conducted before the start of the epidemic season. Notably, 37 healthcare workers (0.1%) were among reported cases. Although the surveillance data do not distinguish occupational from community-acquired infections, the known risk of nosocomial SFTS transmission warrants strict adherence to standard precautions in healthcare settings.

Photo of ticks in lab. Photo: Xinhua

A total of 37 people in East China's Jiangsu Province have been diagnosed with Severe Fever with Thrombocytopenia Syndrome (SFTS) this year, a disease caused by the novel bunya virus which is spread by ticks. Experts have warned that the virus can be transmitted from person to person.

Based on previous cases, the virus can be transmitted from infected animals or people to others via blood, respiratory tract and wounds, Sheng Jifang, an expert on the novel bunya virus and director of the infectious disease department with the First Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang University School of Medicine, told the Global Times on Wednesday.

Sheng mentioned that a patient who was infected with the novel bunya virus three years ago and died later had infected 16 people that had contact with the patient's dead body as the patient had bleeding because of severe infection. One of the infected people later died.

Therefore, medical staff and family members of patients should take necessary preventive and protective measures, Sheng said. She also suggested people should not go into the jungle or bushes. "Fortunately, ticks can't fly. It should be safe just to avoid their territory," Sheng said.

Ticks, from larvae to adults, feed on the blood of warm-blooded animals, according to Sheng. Novel bunya virus infections increase significantly in summer when the ticks breed actively. Therefore, the tick-borne virus could possibly cause a local epidemic.

Sheng said the novel bunya virus, which was first discovered in 2009 in Central China's Henan and East China's Anhui provinces has a fatality rate of 1 percent to 5 percent, and older people are more likely to get sick and die. There is no vaccine or specific medicine targeting the infection, so people need to get treatment as soon as possible once they are infected with the virus.

"The early symptoms are fatigue and fever; sometimes there will be a rash," Sheng said.

The clinical manifestations of SFTS mainly include fever, lower quantities of platelets and white blood cells, and multi-organ dysfunction. Patients with mild cases of this disease can mostly heal themselves, but patients with severe cases often suffer from multi-organ dysfunction or even multi-organ failure.

Ticks are mainly found in mountainous regions, as well as areas where there are wild animals, Leng Peien, director of the vector control division with Shanghai's Municipal Center for Disease Control and Prevention, told the Global Times. Some wetlands and forest parks in the city are also habitats for ticks.

So far, the novel bunya virus infections that have been discovered are mainly caused by tick bites, Leng said.

Ticks can carry many disease-causing viruses, such as Lyme disease and Tsutsugamushi disease, Sheng said. The insect is frequently seen in northeastern and southern regions of China.

Lu'an in East China's Anhui Province confirmed on July 11 that the tick-borne infectious disease SFTS has caused five deaths and hospitalized 23 people in Jinzhai county of the city since April. Qingdao in East China's Shandong Province also reported four deaths, according to a media report in July.

## Abstract

Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) is an emerging infectious disease that was discovered in China in 2010. The causative agent has been identified as a new member of the Phlebovirus genus in the family Bunyaviridae and has been designated severe fever with thrombocytopenia virus (SFTSV). SFTSV infection can be transmitted person-to-person, and the average case fatality rate is approximately 10% in humans. There is a high seroprevalence of SFTSV infection in a wide range of domesticated animals, including sheep, goats, cattle, pigs, dogs and chickens. Ticks are suspected to be the vector that transmits the virus to humans. Currently, the SFTS endemic area is expanding. Therefore, SFTSV infection is an increasingly important public health threat.

Keywords: bunyavirus, emerging infectious disease, phlebovirus, SFTSV

## Introduction

Since 2009, sporadic cases with clinical presentations of fever (≥38 °C), thrombocytopenia, leukocytopenia and gastrointestinal symptoms were frequently reported in rural areas of Hubei, Henan, Jiangsu, Anhui, Liaoning and Shandong provinces in central and northeastern China. Known pathogens that could cause similar symptoms were not detected in the majority of these patients, and initially the reported case fatality rate was 30%. In response to this emerging infectious disease with unknown causes, enhanced surveillance was implemented for severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) in 2010. More than 20 virus strains were isolated from SFTS patients in six provinces of China, and those isolates were identified as the causative pathogen of SFTS and therefore designated as SFTS virus (SFTSV).1,2 According to the surveillance data,3 SFTS cases have been identified in at least 13 provinces in China, and the average case fatality rate of SFTS is approximately 10%.3,4 Moreover, a newly released report in 2012 revealed that two cases of new phlebovirus infections in Missouri in the United States had clinical presentations similar to those of SFTS, and a phylogenetic analysis showed that the novel virus identified in the United States is most closely related to SFTSV.5

## Morphology and genome structure

Viruses in the bunyaviridae family are generally spherical virions or sometimes are elongated, approximately 80–120 nm in diameter, with a lipid bilayer envelope that is 5–7 nm thick.6 SFTSV virions have typical morphologic features of bunyaviruses. Negative-stain electron microscopy of purified SFTSV virions shows that the virus particles are enveloped spheres or ovals with diameters of 80–100 nm.1 The surface projections could be observed on SFTSV virions, and the typical round and closely packed morphologic units on the virion surface further implicate SFTSV as a member of the phlebovirus genus.7 The interior of the virions, as observed by thin section electron microscopy, has a filamentous or coiled bead appearance, which indicates the presence of a helical nucleocapsid structure comprised of the nucleocapsid protein and the viral genome segments.

Like other members of the family Bunyaviridae, SFTSV is an enveloped RNA virus with three single-stranded RNA genomes, consisting of the large (L), medium (M) and small (S) segments.1 The L and M segments are of negative polarity. The L segment contains 6368 nucleotides with one open reading frame encoding the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRP), composed of 2084 amino acids. The M segment contains 3378 nucleotides with one open reading frame encoding 1073 amino acids of the precursor of glycoproteins Gn and Gc. The S segment of SFTSV contains 1744 nucleotides, which uses an ambisense strategy to encode the nucleoprotein (N) in antisense orientation and the nonstructural protein (NSs) in sense orientation, separated by a 54-bp intergenic region. The 5' and 3' termini of the L, M and S segments possess short noncoding sequences. The 5' noncoding regions of SFTSV strain HB29 are 16 nucleotide (nt) (L), 18 nt (M) and 42 nt (S), and the 3' noncoding regions are 100 nt (L), 141 nt (M) and 28 nt (S).

Phylogenetic trees based on complete sequences of the L, M and S segments, from a panel of SFTSV isolates showed that the novel virus is classified in the genus of Phlebovirus, family Bunyaviridae. Further, phylogenetic analysis of the complete deduced amino acid sequences for the RdRp, glycoprotein (Gn and Gc), N and NSs proteins of six SFTSV strains, showed that all SFTSV isolates were clustered together in comparison with other known Phleboviruses, but were almost equally distant from the other two groups, including the sandfly fever group (Rift Valley fever, Punta Toro, Toscana, Massila, sandfly fever Sicilian viruses) and the Uukuniemi group.1,2 The molecular and morphological data suggested SFTS virus to fit the prototype of a new member of the genus Phlebovirus. A comparison of amino acid sequence similarity provided further support of the separation of SFTSV from other Phleboviruses. Both the RdRp and glycoproteins (Gn and Gc) of SFTSV are slightly more closely related to counterparts in Uukuniemi group but only share a maximum similarity of 36%, while the most highly conserved protein of SFTSV, the N protein, only shared 41% similarity with Rift Valley fever virus (RVFV). With more diversity, the S segment-encoded NSs protein of SFTSV showed the lowest amino acid similarity to RVFV, with a value of only 11%–16%. The pairwise comparisons of SFTSV with the newly discovered Heartland virus in the United States showed that the amino acid sequences of the viral RdRp, glycoprotein (Gn and Gc), nucleoprotein, and non-structural protein shared homology of 73.4%, 62.6%, 62.8% and 63.5%, respectively.1

## Epidemiology and transmission

During recent decades, phlebovirus infections have been mainly recorded in Africa and Europe. For major members of the phlebovirus genus, the phlebotomine sandfly-transmitted viruses (Toscana virus, sandfly fever Sicilian viruses, sandfly fever Naples virus), were reported around Mediterranean Europe; mosquito-transmitted RVFV was reported in Africa and the Arabian Peninsula, and the tick-transmitted Uukuniemi virus was mainly distributed in Europe.6,8,9 There had been no reports of identification of phlebovirus in China until the discovery of SFTSV in 2009.

As a newly identified member in the phlebovirus genus, epidemiological findings revealed that most SFTSV cases occur in farmers living in wooded and hilly areas and working in the fields.1,10,11 There is an obvious seasonal distribution of SFTS: the endemic starts around March, peaks between May and July, and ends around November.1,12 The geographic and seasonal distributions, and the tick bite history of some SFTS cases, suggest that ticks were the insect vector to transmit the virus to humans. Studies showed that the tick species Haemaphysalis longicornis were dominant in the endemic regions, and SFTSV RNA was isolated from approximately 4.9% of the total Haemaphysalis longicornis pools collected.13 The nucleic acid sequences of viruses isolated from ticks has 95% homology with the SFTSV isolated from patients.1 These observations suggest that Haemaphysalis longicornis ticks are most likely the major vector of SFTSV.

Current knowledge suggests that many phleboviruses are maintained in their arthropod vectors by vertical (transovarial) transmission and that the vertebrate hosts play little or no role in the basic maintenance cycle of these agents; however, vertebrate hosts may serve as amplifying hosts. Current studies on domesticated animals reported that 47.7% of the animal sera were positive for SFTSV antibodies,14 and 83% of goats in a county in Shandong Province were seropositive for SFTSV.15 Our seroprevalence investigations of more than 3000 domestic animals, with five species in two epidemic regions, found that approximately 70% of sheep, 60% of cattle, 38% of dogs, 3% of pigs and 47% of chickens were SFTSV antibody positive. However, only a small proportion of studied animals (ranging from 1.7% to 5.3%) were found to carry low levels of viral RNA in sera. A genetic analysis of viral isolates from sheep, cattle, dog, and humans revealed a pairwise distance of the S segment of less than 4.6% (unpublished data). Therefore, it seems that there is an intense epizootic of SFTSV in endemic areas, and the domesticated animals might act as amplifying hosts for SFTSV. However, there is a lack of evidence to confirm vertebrate reservoir hosts and to clarify the possibility of vertical transmission in ticks.

Several studies have provided evidence to highlight the risk of person-to-person transmission of SFTSV through direct blood contact with the patient,10,11,16,17 especially when the index patient has a high virus load in the blood,10 with the virus titer in blood of index patients higher than 107 50% tissue culture infective dose/mL. These reports highlight the need to apply strict infection control for suspected clinical SFTS patients and to emphasize the appropriate use of personal protective equipment (PPE) when treating SFTS patients.

## Clinical features

Most phlebovirus human infections are self-limited, resulting in a mild febrile illness.6 Clinical presentations of SFTS patients are non-specific; major symptoms include high fever, thrombocytopenia, leukocytopenia, gastrointestinal symptoms, and lymphadenopathy. Laboratory tests of SFTS patients commonly show elevated serum alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase (AST), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), creatine kinase (CK), creatine kinase MB fraction (CK-MB) levels, as well as a prolonged activated partial-thromboplastin time. These laboratory parameters are indicative of pathological lesions involved in the liver, kidney and coagulation systems of SFTS patients.1,10,18,19 In severe SFTS patients, the clinical conditions may proceed quickly and end in multi-organ dysfunction syndrome, with clinical presentations of central nervous system (CNS) symptoms and hemorrhagic manifestations. Patients commonly die of disseminated intravascular coagulation and multi-organ failure.1,10,18,19

Dynamic monitoring of the disease course identified three major disease stages of SFTS patients:18 the fever stage, the multi-organ dysfunction stage and the convalescent stage. During the first stage of the disease, day 1 to day 7 post-onset of illness, the initial serum viral load was high (average 105–106 copies/mL) and comparable in both fatal and non-fatal cases. Most SFTS cases in both groups had fever, marked thrombocytopenia and leukocytopenia in this stage. In addition, the alanine aminotransferase, AST, LDH, CK and CK-MB levels began to be elevated later during this stage. The second stage was between day 7 and day 13 post-disease onset. During this stage, the serum viral load decreased in non-fatal cases but still remained high in fatal cases (average 108 copies/mL). Coincident with the respective levels of viral load in non-fatal and fatal cases, the platelet counts reverted to a normal range in non-fatal cases but continued to decline in fatal cases. The levels of the serum enzymes AST, LDH, CK and CK-MB began to decline at approximately day 9 or day 11 in non-fatal cases but progressively increased in fatal cases. When the disease proceeded to the third stage after day 13, for most non-fatal cases, the patients could recover from the disease with most clinical parameters converting to normal. However, for fatal cases, the patients died of severe multi-organ dysfunction syndrome and disseminated intravascular coagulation during this stage, and the serum enzymes reached very high levels before death. The risk analysis revealed that high serum levels of AST (>400 U/L), LDH (>800 U/L), CK (>1000 U/L), and CK-MB (>50 U/L) were risk factors associated with death of SFTS patients.18

In the acute phase of SFTS human disease, the levels of a broad spectrum of serum cytokines, interleukin (IL)-1RA, IL-6, IL-10, granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF), interferon-γ-induced protein 10, and monocyte chemotactic protein-1, were elevated in SFTS patients and were present at higher levels in fatal cases compared to non-fatal cases.19,20 In contrast, levels of the cytokines platelet-derived growth factor-BB and regulated and normal T cell expressed and secreted decreased in SFTS patients. These eight cytokines reverted to normal during the convalescent phase of SFTSV infection. The cytokines IL-1β, IL-8, Macrophage inflammatory protein (MIP)-1α and MIP-1β showed a unique pattern of elevation in fatal cases but not in non-fatal cases. However, the levels of these cytokines increased in the convalescent phase of non-fatal SFTS cases. The regression analysis further revealed that the serum viral load correlated with the serum levels of these cytokines. Moreover, the levels of these cytokines correlated with various clinical parameters.20 These findings suggest that the high viral load may lead to an overproduction of proinflammatory cytokines, which could further exacerbate disease severity. Another study reported the elevation of IL-6, IL-10, G-CSF, interferon-γ, and acute phase proteins (phospholipase A, fibrinogen, hepcidin) in SFTS patients, and a higher production of IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, G-CSF, interferon-γ and phospholipase A in fatal SFTS cases than in non-fatal SFTS cases. The study also showed correlations between the viral load and host biomarkers indicative of fatal outcome, including liver enzymes AST, coagulation factors of activated partial-thromboplastin time, thrombin time and fibrinogen, as well as acute phase proteins phospholipase A and hepcidin.19

## Pathology and pathogenesis in animal models

Currently, an infectious C57BL/6 mouse model with hallmark symptoms of thrombocytopenia and leukocytopenia has been established through intramuscular injection of SFTSV into adult mice. In this murine model, viral RNA was detected in the blood, spleen, liver, and kidney. The humoral immune responses of virus-specific IgM and IgG, neutralizing antibodies, and cellular responses were efficiently induced in the SFTSV-infected mice.21

Histopathological changes were identified in the spleen and bone marrow in the early phase of infection, and pathological lesions in the liver and kidney developed in a later stage. In the SFTSV infected spleen, the lymphocyte cellularity of the red pulp was visually decreased during the first week after inoculation and gradually recovered 14 days later. In addition, a marked increase of megakaryocytes was observed in the spleen. Similarly, megakaryocytes in the bone marrow also significantly increased in the early stage of infection. This increase of platelet progenitor cells in principle and secondary hematopoietic organs suggests extramedullary hematopoiesis may compensate for the depletion of circulating platelets. During the late phase of SFTSV infection, pathological changes were noted in the liver and kidney. The primary lesions in the liver consisted of ballooning degeneration of hepatocytes and scattered necrosis. The lesions in kidney typically included glomerular hypercellularity, mesangial thickening, and congestion in Bowman's space, while infiltration of inflammatory cells was absent. Pathological changes within the liver and kidney tissues were maximal on day 14 post-infection but had nearly recovered on day 28 post-infection. Therefore, the pathological features observed in the spleen and bone marrow during the early stage of infection were consistent with the hematological changes of thrombocytopenia and leukocytopenia.21 The transient pathologic changes observed in kidney and liver at the later stage of infection were indicative of acute glomerular nephritis and acute hepatitis with self-limiting outcomes.

The viral RNA load and infectious titers increased in the spleen on day 3 post-infection, which suggests the spleen as the principle target organ for SFTSV replication.21 Focusing on the spleen, we found that the number of macrophages and platelets dramatically increased in the infected spleen, and SFTSV colocalized with platelets in the cytoplasm of macrophages in the red pulp of the spleen. In vitro cellular assays further revealed that SFTSV adhered to platelets and facilitated the phagocytosis of platelets by macrophages, which, in combination with in vivo findings, suggests that the SFTSV-induced thrombocytopenia was caused by clearance of circulating virus-bound platelets promoted by splenic macrophages. Thus, the study elucidated pathology and pathogenic mechanisms of thrombocytopenia in a murine model that resembles human SFTS disease.21

The SFTSV infection in the established C57BL/6 mouse model could mimic major pathological changes of clinical infection in patients; however, lethal infection has only been induced in certain strains of newborn mice22 but not in adult rodent models. It is suspected that the severe infection could only be induced in immune incompetent hosts, such as newborn mice, without a completely mature immune system, or certain strains of immune-deficient mice.

## Laboratory diagnosis

In most phlebovirus infections, the diagnosis is based on serological tests.8,9 In-house enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) methods are developed, commonly including IgM capture ELISA in acute phase serum or by IgG sandwich ELISA in paired sera from acute and convalescent phases.23 Neutralization assays using early convalescent sera remain the reference method to specifically identify the viruses or to assess the antibody response specificity. Virologic diagnosis of RVFV infection is through detection of viremia in the acute phase of illness, initially using intracranial inoculation into suckling mice or infection of susceptible cells (Vero or mosquito cells) to grow the virus.6 More recently, detection of serum or blood viral RNA copies by reverse transcription-PCR amplification has been developed and was found to be very useful for rapid presumptive diagnosis,24 which could be followed by sequencing to further characterize the viral strains.

Currently, a variety of assays have been developed for laboratory diagnosis of infections with SFTSV. The early viral nucleic acid detection is performed by one-step Taqman real-time assays, using the highly conserved regions of all three genome segments L, M and S of SFTSV as targets.25 Commonly, the viral nucleic acids can be detected in the acute phase serum of patients, within 2 weeks post-onset of the disease. The sensitivity and specificity of the assay is 98.6% and 99%, respectively.25 The real-time PCR assay, based on the S segment, has been approved by the State Food and Drug Administration for application in clinical diagnosis in hospitals and disease surveillance by the local Center for Disease Control and Prevention. With respect to the detection of viral nucleic acids using simple instruments and saving time, a reverse transcription loop-mediated isothermal amplification assay to target eight distinct regions on the S segment of SFTSV has been developed. When combined with a fluorescent detection reagent, visible results could be determined by showing a color change within 30 min.26 Another similar assay, which incorporates reverse transcription-cross-priming amplification with a vertical flow visualization strip based on the M segment of the SFTSV, could complete the entire procedure from specimen processing to result reporting within 2 h.27 As for serodiagnosis, the in-house Mac-ELISA assay, indirect ELISA assay, and double antigen sandwich ELISA assay have been established and optimized to test virus specific IgM, IgG and total antibodies in serum samples of patients, respectively.1,14 Indirect immunofluorescence assays were also established to test the virus specific antibodies using previously fixed SFTSV infected cells on slides. # Bandavirus (taxid:2733256)

Formerly named Banyangvirus

#### VIRION

Enveloped, spherical. Diameter from 80 to 120nm. Glycoproteins at the surface of the envelope are arranged on an icosahedral lattice, with T=12 symmetry.

#### GENOME

Segmented Negative-stranded RNA linear genome, L segment is about 6.4kb, M segment about 3.4kb and S segment about 1.7kb.  
Encodes for six proteins.

#### GENE EXPRESSION

**Transcription** starts by viral RNA dependent RNA polymerase (L) binding to a promoter on each encapsidated segment, and is terminated by a strong hairpin sequence at the end of each gene. These are capped by L protein during synthesis using cap snatching , but are not polyadenylated.
  
S segment uses ambisense strategy to encode for several proteins: both genomic and antigenomic RNA are transcribed. The hairpin sequence is a stop polymerase signal which prevents ambisense transcription from producing dsRNA.

#### ENZYMES

#### REPLICATION

**CYTOPLASMIC**

1. Virus attaches to host receptors though Gn-Gc glycoprotein dimer, and is endocytosed into vesicles in the host cell.
2. Fusion of virus membrane with the vesicle membrane; ribonucleocapsid segments are released in the cytoplasm.
3. Transcription, viral mRNAs are capped in the cytoplasm.
4. Replication presumably starts when enough nucleoprotein is present to encapsidate neo-synthetized antigenomes and genomes.
5. The ribonucleocapsids buds at Golgi apparatus, releasing the virion by exocytosis.

## Abstract

### Background

Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) incidence has risen steadily in China since the disease was first identified in 2009, with both case numbers and the geographic scope of reporting expanding over time. This study analyzed national surveillance data from 2010 to 2024 to characterize the evolving epidemiological patterns of SFTS.

### Methods

This retrospective descriptive study included clinically diagnosed and laboratory-confirmed SFTS cases from China Information System for Disease Control and Prevention (CISDCP) (2010–2024). Joinpoint regression was used to analyze incidence trends. Case fatality rate (CFR) differences were assessed by chi-squared or Fisher’s exact tests, and the temporal trend was assessed by linear regression.

### Results

During 2010–2024, a total of 30 provinces reported 34,055 cases. From 2010 to 2024, the incidence rate of SFTS in China showed a fluctuating upward trend, with an average annual percent change (AAPC) of 43.28% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 43.23%–43.33%;*P* < 0.01). Most cases were sporadic, with some regional clustering and rapid geographic expansion to previously unaffected areas. The number of reported cases in Anhui Province began to rise rapidly in 2022, making it the province with the highest number of reported cases in China in 2023 and 2024. The average CFR was 4.79%, and the CFR increased with age, reaching 9.15% among those aged 85 years and above.

### Conclusions

During the period from 2010 to 2024, SFTS in China exhibited a marked increase in reported incidence and considerable geographical expansion. The disease is no longer confined to traditional high-risk areas; the rapid rise in cases in province such as Anhui suggests a critical need to re-evaluate the ecological and social factors driving its transmission. Although the overall population CFR showed a declining trend, mortality risk among elderly subgroups still needs attention.

## Background

Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) is an acute viral infectious disease mainly characterized by fever and thrombocytopenia caused by *Dabie bandavirus* (SFTS virus) [1]. It is also characterized by obvious bleeding tendencies accompanied by leukopenia and multiple organ dysfunction [2]. Clinical manifestations are often atypical; no licensed vaccine or specific antiviral therapy is currently available, and clinical management mainly relies on supportive care [3, 4]. SFTS was classified as a nationally reportable disease in China in 2010 and was listed by the World Health Organization(WHO) as one of the top 10 priority infectious diseases in the 2017 annual review of diseases prioritized under the Research and Development Blueprint [5, 6]. The WHO released a prioritization of future pathogens of concern on July 30, 2024, in which the priority pathogens of concern for the Western Pacific region include the *Dabie bandavirus* [7]. This designation underscores the global health importance of SFTS and the need for up-to-date epidemiological data to inform international surveillance efforts. Effective April 1, 2026, SFTS was reclassified as a Class B notifiable infectious disease [8].

Tick bites are the main mode of transmission of the disease. Transmission can also occur through contact with the blood, bloody secretions, excretions, or contaminated materials of infected patients, leading to human-to-human transmission and clusters of cases in household or healthcare settings [9]. People who live and work in mountainous, hilly, or forested areas in endemic regions face a higher risk of infection [10]. Healthcare workers, family members, visitors of patients, and mortuary personnel are at higher risk of infection if they do not adhere to standard protective measures [11].

In addition to China, locally infected cases have been reported in Japan, South Korea, Vietnam, Thailand, Myanmar, Pakistan, and other regions, of which Japan and South Korea have reported the highest number of cases [12,13,14,15,16,17,18]. Due to climate change, there has been an expansion of the potential habitat of ticks to wider geographical locations, posing a risk of introducing the exotic tick species that may carry the SFTS virus [19, 20].

Previous national analyses have characterized the epidemiology of SFTS in China for periods through 2021 or 2023 [21,22,23]. However, no study has examined the complete 15-year surveillance record from SFTS’s initial emergence through 2024, a period that now includes record case and death counts, continued geographic expansion to 30 of 31 mainland provinces. To address this gap, this study analyzed national SFTS surveillance data from 2010 to 2024 to characterize temporal trends, geographic expansion, seasonal patterns, population distribution, time intervals between onset and diagnosis, and case fatality rates (CFR).

## Materials and methods

### Study design

This was a retrospective descriptive study of national surveillance data.

### Data source

SFTS data and annual population data were obtained from the China Information System for Disease Control and Prevention (CISDCP), excluding Hong Kong SAR, Macao SAR, and Taiwan Province [24]. We included cases with onset dates between January 1, 2010, and December 31, 2024. Each case was confirmed by laboratory testing or diagnosed clinically [21, 22, 25]. Case classification followed the diagnosis and treatment scheme for severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (2023 Edition), which had been consistently applied in practice before its official release [26]. The dataset included demographic variables (age, sex, occupation, residence), dates of onset, diagnosis, and death, and case classification.

### Statistical analysis

Data were processed, statistically analyzed, and visualized using Microsoft Excel 2016 and R software (version 4.4.2). No observations were excluded from this analysis.

Joinpoint regression was used to analyze temporal trends in annual SFTS incidence rates. A log-linear model was fitted, allowing a maximum of two joinpoints. The optimal number of joinpoints was selected using the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC). The annual percent change (APC) for each segment was calculated as (exp(β) − 1) × 100%, and the average annual percent change (AAPC) was computed as the weighted average of segment-specific APCs. The 95% confidence intervals (CI) for APCs and AAPC were derived using the Delta method, with statistical inference under the t-distribution. Analyses were performed using R software version 4.4.2.

The onset-to-diagnosis interval was calculated as the number of days between symptom onset date and diagnosis date, as recorded in CISDCP. Given the right-skewed distribution (except in 2010), the median and interquartile range (IQR; 25th percentile [P25]–75th percentile [P75]) were used as summary measures, as they are robust to extreme values.

Deaths were identified based on CISDCP records for reported SFTS cases. The CFR was calculated as deaths/reported cases × 100%. The 95% CI were estimated using the Wilson score method. Group differences were assessed by chi-squared or Fisher’s exact tests, and the temporal trend was assessed by linear regression.

## Results

### National temporal trends

From 2010 to 2024, a total of 34,055 SFTS cases were reported across 30 provinces in China. The number of reported cases (6,602 cases) and deaths (306 cases) in 2024 were both the highest levels since the discovery of this disease, with an increase of 30.4% and 60.2% respectively, compared to the reported cases (5061 cases) and deaths (191 cases) in 2023 (Fig. 1).

Temporal distribution of SFTS cases in China from 2010 to 2024

Among 34,055 SFTS cases recorded from 2010 to 2024, 21.1% (7,190) were clinically diagnosed and 78.9% (26,865) were laboratory‑confirmed. In 2024, the proportion of laboratory‑confirmed cases reached its highest level at 95.3% (Fig. 2).

**Fig. 2**

Classification distribution of SFTS cases in China from 2010 to 2024

From 2010 to 2024, the incidence rate of SFTS in China showed a fluctuating upward trend, with an AAPC of 43.28%, and the difference was statistically significant (95% CI: 43.23%–43.33%; *P* < 0.01). Joinpoint regression identified 2012 as the single inflection point. The incidence rate increased rapidly from 2010 to 2012 (APC = 218.14%, 95% CI: 217.75%–218.52%; *P* < 0.01), followed by a sustained increase from 2012 to 2024 (APC = 14.14%, 95% CI: 14.09%–14.19%; *P* < 0.01).

### Geographic expansion

The geographic range of reported SFTS cases expanded from 17 counties in 5 provinces in 2010 to 459 counties in 24 provinces in 2024, and exhibited geographically discontinuous emergence of reported cases. By 2024, cases had been reported in 30 of China’s 31 mainland provincial-level administrative divisions, with Ningxia being the sole exception, cumulatively affecting 759 counties nationwide (Fig. 3).

### Changes in provincial burden

From 2010 to 2024, cases were mainly concentrated in 7 provinces, including Shandong (9,547 cases), Anhui (7,494 cases), Henan (7,148 cases), Hubei (5,068 cases), Liaoning (1,857 cases), Jiangsu (1,384 cases), and Zhejiang (1,153 cases), with the cumulative number of reported cases accounting for 98.8% of all nationally reported cases. The annual case distribution across these seven provinces exhibited distinct temporal dynamics (Fig. 4). In the early phase (2010–2013), case numbers remained relatively low across all provinces. Shandong and Henan experienced rapid increases beginning in 2014, with Henan reaching its peak during 2015–2016 (976 and 879 cases, respectively). Shandong maintained a relatively high level throughout the period, with a notable surge in 2024 (1,658 cases). The number of reported cases in Anhui Province began to rise rapidly in 2022, making it the province with the highest number of reported cases in China in 2023 and 2024. The number of reported cases in Anhui rose from 544 in 2021 to 841 in 2022, 1,416 in 2023, and reached 1,777 in 2024.

### Seasonal patterns

The incidence of SFTS is seasonal, with a gradual increase in the number of cases from March each year, a peak in May-July, and a decreasing trend thereafter; a secondary increase in case counts was observed in October in some provinces. The cumulative number of reported cases in the months of April-October from 2010 to 2024 was 32,963, accounting for 96.8% of the cumulative number of reported cases in the whole year from 2010 to 2024 (Fig. 5). Different provinces exhibited distinct seasonal patterns. Liaoning showed a later peak (July-September), while Shandong peaked during May-August. A secondary increase in case counts was observed in October in Anhui, Hubei, and Jiangsu provinces.

### Population distribution

Cases were reported in all age groups, mainly in people aged 40–84 years (94.3%), mainly farmers (83.5%), slightly more females than males, and the male-to-female ratio was 0.89:1. The CFR increased with age (Fig. 6). Notably, 37 healthcare workers (0.1%) were among reported cases.

### Time intervals between onset and diagnosis

With the exception of 2010 (skewness − 0.12), the distribution of onset-to-diagnosis intervals was right-skewed in all years (skewness range: 2.34–13.97), supporting the use of median rather than mean. The overall median onset-to-diagnosis interval over the 15-year period was 7 days (Interquartile Range [IQR]: 4–11). Annual median intervals and IQRs are shown in Fig. 7. A declining trend was observed from 2010 to 2012, followed by an increase in 2014. From 2015 to 2024, the interval had decreased again, reaching a median of 5 days.

### CFR analysis

From 2010 to 2024, a total of 1,632 deaths were recorded among 34,055 reported cases, yielding an overall CFR of 4.79%. The national CFR declined significantly from 12.68% in 2010 to 4.63% in 2024 (linear trend, *P* = 0.004; Fig. 8). The CFR increased with age, from 0.29% in the 30–34 age group to 9.15% in those aged ≥ 85 years (*P* < 0.001). Males had a higher CFR than females (5.41% vs. 4.24%, *P* < 0.001). Laboratory-confirmed cases showed a higher CFR than clinically diagnosed cases (5.55% vs. 1.95%, *P* < 0.001). Substantial provincial variation was observed (*P* < 0.001), with CFRs among seven provinces with the highest case counts ranging from 2.25% (Henan) to 11.97% (Zhejiang).
